mcqs.question: Without a state file, what happens when Terraform runs against a resource block for infrastructure that already exists?
options: Terraform automatically detects and adopts it
Terraform refuses to run at all
Terraform has no way to know it corresponds to existing infrastructure and would try to create a new one
Terraform queries the cloud provider to reconstruct state automatically on every plan
mcqs.explanation: State is the mapping between a resource block and a real-world object's ID — without it, Terraform has no record of that link and would attempt to create a duplicate rather than manage the existing one. This is exactly why terraform import exists, to establish that mapping manually.

mcqs.question: Why is local state a risk for a team, even if each engineer runs Terraform correctly?
options: Local state is slower to read than remote state
Terraform doesn't support local state for team projects
Local state can't store resource attributes at all
Two engineers can silently overwrite each other's state changes, since there's no shared, locked source of truth
mcqs.explanation: The risk isn't performance or a missing feature — it's that each engineer has their own copy of a file meant to be a single source of truth, so concurrent or out-of-order applies can clobber each other's changes. A remote backend with locking is what prevents this specific failure mode.

mcqs.question: After running `terraform import` on a manually-created resource, what's still required before `plan` shows no unexpected changes?
options: The matching HCL resource block must accurately reflect the real resource's actual configuration
Nothing — import fully generates and configures everything automatically
The resource must be destroyed and recreated by Terraform
A remote backend must be configured first
mcqs.explanation: Import only wires up the state-to-reality mapping — it's on you to write (or verify) an HCL resource block whose attributes actually match the real resource. A mismatch surfaces the next plan as Terraform proposing to 'fix' every attribute you got wrong, not as an import failure.

mcqs.question: A plan shows Terraform wanting to recreate a resource that's actually running fine. What's the safest first diagnostic step?
options: Apply the plan immediately to resolve the mismatch
Manually hand-edit the JSON state file to match reality
Run terraform plan -refresh-only to see the discrepancy between state and the actual API without proposing resource changes
Delete the state file and start over
mcqs.explanation: A refresh-only plan safely surfaces exactly what's out of sync between recorded state and real infrastructure without threatening to change anything. Applying the misleading plan risks real damage, hand-editing JSON state risks corrupting other entries, and deleting state loses Terraform's entire record of what it manages.
